WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Throughout her career, singer-songwriter Cyndi Lauper has promoted gay and lesbian rights. She has a personal connection to this cause -- her sister is a lesbian -- but she also believes it's a matter of fairness. Cyndi Lauper worked with Cathy Nelson of the Human Rights Campaign to raise awareness of LGBT issues. "It's always wrong to discriminate," the Grammy Award winner said. "I grew up in the civil rights movement. It was wrong then, and it is wrong now." With her 2007 and 2008 "True Colors" tours, Lauper has helped raise awareness about lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights around the country. She said fellow LGBT activist Cathy Nelson especially motivates her. Nelson worked at the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), a national LGBT civil rights organization, and her dedication to those issues runs deep. Fighting for fairness and equality, she said, drives her. "I'm a lesbian, and I see the issues very personally," Nelson said. "When it deep-down resonates that you don't have the same rights and responsibilities, or people don't view you the same, it can be demoralizing and empowering at the same time." Nelson's passion for the cause has enabled her to inspire thousands of people across the country to get involved. When she was growing up in rural Illinois, Nelson said, she hadn't imagined following this path. She trained to be a teacher, but on a whim, became a flight attendant with Eastern Airlines to fulfill her "intense desire to travel." In the 1980s, she became involved with labor issues through her flight attendant union. That led to working on women's issues with the National Organization of Women in Washington. In 1989, she started working for the HRC. Since then, she has helped bring LGBT rights out of the closet and onto the national stage. Hired to increase the group's membership, Nelson built a strong volunteer network in communities across the nation. HRC had just 12,000 members when Nelson started. Today it has more than 725,000, making it the largest gay and lesbian rights organization in the country. "Part of my job is getting people to be vocal," Nelson said. "It's important that everyone has an understanding that discrimination is happening every single day against a certain segment of society. And that's just wrong." In 2007, when Lauper worked with HRC for the "True Colors" tour, she and Nelson teamed up to bring gay and straight audiences together on fairness and equality issues. Nelson realized it was also an opportunity to shine the spotlight on an issue she'd worked on for almost a decade -- the passage of a hate crimes bill that would make attacks based on sexual orientation, disability, or gender a federal crime. For Nelson, crimes against LGBT people -- such as the murder of Matthew Shepard -- represent the darkest side of ignorance on these issues. In 2006, more than one in six hate crimes were committed against LGBT individuals, an 18 percent rise over the previous year, according to the FBI. "I learned from Cathy that hate crimes send fear through a community," Lauper said. "You could die just because of who you are."  Watch Lauper and Nelson talk about the "True Colors" tour to raise awareness » . At every concert, Lauper spoke passionately about the need to pass the bill, and her song, "True Colors," was used in a public service announcement about the legislation. HRC volunteers distributed information at each venue and had postcards on hand for people to send to their legislators. In the end, more than 15,000 people signed postcards, and both houses of Congress passed the bill by wide margins. Although President Bush never signed the bill, Nelson and Lauper have high hopes for it to soon become law. For Nelson, getting so many people engaged was a key achievement. "The biggest reward for me is when I've played some part in empowering someone to get involved," she said. Lauper knows first-hand how convincing Nelson can be. "The fact that you can actually succeed and help people -- you really get that from her," she said. "People like Cathy get all of us motivated."

# The Activist Behind the Music: Cathy Nelson's Journey with True Colors

*A CNN Profile*

There's a particular kind of energy that fills a room when Cathy Nelson talks about the intersection of music and activism. As a longtime advocate with the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), Nelson has spent years working at the crossroads of pop culture and policy—and few projects capture that fusion quite like the True Colors tour.

## A Partnership Built on Purpose

When Cyndi Lauper launched the True Colors tour, it wasn't just another concert series. It was conceived as a vehicle for change, bringing together musicians and LGBTQ advocacy organizations to raise both awareness and resources for equality efforts across the country. Nelson's work with HRC placed her squarely in the middle of that mission, helping bridge the gap between entertainment and grassroots organizing.

"Music has this unique power to open hearts before it opens minds," Nelson has often reflected in describing the philosophy behind the tour. "You get thousands of people in an arena, and suddenly the issues aren't abstract anymore—they're personal."

## Turning Concerts Into Conversations

The True Colors tour became known for more than its star-studded lineups. Between sets, attendees encountered voter registration tables, educational materials about LGBTQ rights, and volunteers—many mobilized through Nelson's efforts—ready to talk about everything from marriage equality to anti-discrimination legislation.

For Nelson, the work went beyond a single tour date or a single summer. It reflected HRC's broader strategy of meeting people where they already were emotionally invested, using shared cultural moments as entry points into civic engagement.

## A Legacy of Coalition-Building

What made Nelson's contributions notable within advocacy circles was her ability to translate star power into sustained action. Concerts end, but campaigns for equal rights don't—and much of Nelson's role involved ensuring that the enthusiasm generated by artists like Lauper translated into concrete organizing: petition signatures, local chapter growth, and pressure on lawmakers.

Lauper herself has been vocal about why these partnerships mattered to her personally, often citing family members and friends within the LGBTQ community as her motivation for lending her platform to the cause. Nelson's role was to ensure that motivation had infrastructure behind it.

## Continuing Impact

Years after the tour's most prominent runs, the model pioneered by True Colors—pairing celebrity visibility with grassroots advocacy—remains a template referenced in discussions of effective cultural organizing. Nelson's contributions, often working behind the scenes rather than on stage, exemplify the kind of sustained institutional work that transforms a moment of cultural attention into lasting policy change.

---

**A Pop Icon's Enduring Commitment to Equality**

Cyndi Lauper, the Grammy-winning artist known for anthems like "True Colors" and "Girls Just Want to Have Fun," has long been recognized as one of music's most dedicated allies to the LGBTQ community. Her activism, which spans decades, has recently intensified through a close working partnership with Cathy Nelson, a staffer at the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), the nation's largest LGBTQ civil rights organization.

Together, Lauper and Nelson have been pushing for stronger hate crimes legislation, working to ensure that violence motivated by anti-LGBTQ bias is prosecuted with the seriousness it demands under federal and state law.

**The Partnership with Cathy Nelson**

Nelson, who has worked within HRC's advocacy infrastructure, has helped connect Lauper's celebrity platform with the organization's policy expertise. The collaboration reflects a broader trend of artists using their cultural capital to support grassroots and legislative efforts rather than merely lending their name to causes symbolically.

Sources close to the partnership describe a genuine working relationship in which Lauper has taken an active role — participating in briefings, attending rallies, and using her media appearances to draw attention to specific legislative pushes rather than speaking only in general terms about equality.

**Why Hate Crimes Legislation Matters**

Hate crimes legislation has remained a central priority for LGBTQ advocacy organizations for years, particularly efforts to expand protections to explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories. Advocates argue that without such explicit inclusion, crimes motivated by anti-LGBTQ animus can be prosecuted inconsistently or without acknowledgment of the bias motivating them.

Lauper has spoken publicly about the urgency of this issue, framing it not as a partisan matter but as a fundamental question of safety and dignity. Her "True Colors" tour and foundation have historically funneled resources toward LGBTQ homelessness and equality initiatives, and her current legislative push builds on that foundation.

**A Broader Legacy of Advocacy**

This is far from Lauper's first foray into LGBTQ activism. She co-founded the True Colors Fund (now merged into other LGBTQ youth homelessness initiatives) and has been a fixture at Pride events, benefit concerts, and legislative rallies for years. Her willingness to embed herself in the granular policy work — rather than simply showing up for high-visibility moments — has earned her respect among advocacy professionals.

"Cyndi doesn't just want to sing about acceptance," one HRC associate noted. "She wants to see it written into law."

**Looking Ahead**

As hate crimes legislation continues to be debated in various state legislatures and in Congress, Lauper and Nelson's partnership signals a continued push to keep LGBTQ safety at the forefront of the national conversation. With her combination of star power and sustained commitment, Lauper remains one of the most visible celebrity advocates translating cultural influence into legislative action.

# When Music Meets Movement: How a Songwriter and an Activist Found Common Cause in the Fight Against Hate

*A story of unlikely partnership, personal loss, and the power of showing up*

---

The first time Maria Santos heard "Still Standing," she was sitting in her car outside a grocery store in Columbus, Ohio, unable to turn off the ignition. The song had come on the radio unannounced — no introduction, no context — just a voice singing about a brother who never made it home.

Santos, who has spent the better part of two decades organizing for LGBT rights, didn't know then that the song's writer would become one of her closest collaborators. She didn't know that within a year, they'd be standing together on statehouse steps, in television studios, and eventually in the halls of Congress, pushing lawmakers to strengthen hate crimes protections.

"I just remember thinking, someone else understands this grief," Santos said. "Not the political version of it. The real version."

## A Song Born From Silence

Singer-songwriter Jesse Calloway wrote "Still Standing" three years ago, in the aftermath of losing a close friend to a violent attack that investigators initially — and, Calloway insists, willfully — declined to classify as a hate crime.

"They kept saying there wasn't enough evidence of motive," Calloway said, sitting in the small Nashville studio where much of his recent work has taken shape. "But we knew. His friends knew. The community knew. It was never really a mystery to us — it was a mystery to people who didn't want to see it."

Calloway, who is gay and had spent much of his early career avoiding songs that referenced his identity too directly, said something shifted after that loss.

"I'd built a career on being vague enough that everyone could relate, which is really just a nice way of saying I was scared," he said. "After that, vague wasn't an option anymore."

"Still Standing" was released quietly, without a major label push, almost as an afterthought to a larger album. It found its audience anyway — first through word of mouth, then through LGBT advocacy circles, and eventually through Santos, who began using it as the closing track at rallies she organized across the Midwest.

## From Fan to Partner

Santos didn't set out to become an activist. She stumbled into the work in her mid-twenties, after a cousin was assaulted outside a bar in what police reports described only as a "dispute." The word "hate crime" appeared nowhere in the paperwork, despite witnesses who said otherwise.

"That was my education," Santos said. "You learn very fast how much language matters in these systems, and how much gets lost when the people writing the reports don't understand what they're looking at."

She began organizing informally, then formally, eventually founding a regional advocacy network focused specifically on improving how hate crimes are documented, investigated, and prosecuted — an area she describes as "unglamorous but foundational."

When she reached out to Calloway's team about using his song at events, she expected, at best, a licensing agreement. Instead, Calloway asked to meet her.

"I wanted to know if this was something I could actually be part of, not just adjacent to," Calloway said. "I didn't want to be the guy who wrote a sad song and then disappeared."

## Turning a Partnership Into a Platform

What followed was an 18-month collaboration that neither anticipated. Calloway began performing at Santos' rallies, sometimes solo with just a guitar, sometimes joined by local choirs assembled for the occasion. Santos, in turn, began opening those same events with testimony — not policy statements, but personal stories, hers and others', about what happens when systems fail to name what they're looking at.

"Jesse brings people in who would never come to a rally," Santos said. "And once they're there, they're not just there for the music."

Their work culminated in testimony before a state legislative committee considering an expansion of hate crimes statutes to include more robust training requirements for law enforcement — a provision Santos had pushed for years, with limited traction, before Calloway's involvement helped generate broader public attention.

The bill passed in a narrow but bipartisan vote.

"I don't think the song passed the bill," Calloway said, careful not to overstate his role. "But I think it made people willing to sit in a room and listen to Maria in a way they might not have otherwise."

Santos is less modest on his behalf. "Music does something testimony alone can't do," she said. "It gets past people's defenses before they even realize they've let it in."

## What Comes Next

The two are now working on a documentary project chronicling the broader effort to reform how hate crimes are tracked and prosecuted nationally, with Calloway's music serving as connective tissue between interviews with survivors, families, and lawmakers.

Both are careful to note that the work is unfinished, and that legislative wins in one state don't translate automatically elsewhere.

"There are a dozen more states where this same fight is starting from zero," Santos said. "The song can travel faster than I can. That's the whole point of doing this together."

For Calloway, the shift from private songwriter to public advocate remains, he admits, uncomfortable at times.

"I didn't become a musician to give speeches," he said. "But I also didn't become a musician to stay quiet while people I love are still being erased from the reports."

Santos, listening nearby, nodded. "That's the whole thing, isn't it," she said. "Neither one of us set out to do this. We just couldn't figure out how not to."

# Voices for Justice: The "True Colors" Tour Amplifies Personal Stories in Fight for Hate Crimes Protection

When Cyndi Lauper takes the stage each night on the "True Colors" tour, she's not just performing the songs that made her a pop icon in the 1980s. She's channeling decades of personal conviction into a cause that has become deeply woven into her identity as an artist and activist.

The tour, which brings together an eclectic lineup of musicians in support of LGBT rights, centers on a specific legislative goal: passage of federal hate crimes protections that would extend legal safeguards to individuals targeted because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. But behind the concert lights and celebrity headliners are deeply human stories—of loss, advocacy, and the belief that music can move hearts before it moves policy.

## A Personal Anthem Becomes a Rallying Cry

For Lauper, the connection to LGBT rights isn't a recent development or a calculated career move. She has spoken openly over the years about growing up around gay friends and family members, and about the particular anguish of watching people she loved navigate a world that too often refused to protect or even acknowledge them.

Her song "True Colors," originally a tender ballad about accepting oneself despite judgment from others, has been adopted as an unofficial anthem within LGBT communities for decades. By naming her tour after the song, Lauper deliberately created a bridge between her artistic legacy and her activism—transforming a personal hit into a platform for collective action.

"It's about people feeling safe enough to show who they really are," Lauper has said in various interviews about the tour's mission, a sentiment that captures both the song's original meaning and its new political urgency.

## Cathy Nelson: Turning Grief and Advocacy Into Action

Behind the scenes, much of the tour's organizational muscle comes from the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), the nation's largest LGBT advocacy organization. Cathy Nelson, working with HRC, has been instrumental in ensuring the tour doesn't just entertain—it educates and mobilizes.

Nelson's role involves the less glamorous but equally vital work of activism: setting up voter registration tables at venues, coordinating with local LGBT organizations in each tour city, and making sure concertgoers leave not just humming along to hit songs but understanding the stakes of pending federal legislation.

For Nelson and others working alongside her, the hate crimes bill isn't an abstract policy debate. It's connected to real names and real tragedies—cases where individuals were violently targeted because of who they were, and where existing law offered insufficient recourse or recognition of the bias motivating the violence.

The federal hate crimes legislation the tour supports would expand protections to explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, closing gaps that advocates say leave LGBT individuals vulnerable and send a message that crimes against them are treated with less urgency.

## Music as a Bridge to Policy

What makes "True Colors" distinctive among benefit concerts is its explicit pairing of entertainment with direct civic engagement. Attendees aren't simply asked to enjoy a show and perhaps donate to a cause—they're given concrete information about contacting legislators, understanding the bill's provisions, and recognizing how hate crimes legislation intersects with broader questions of equality.

This approach reflects a broader strategy increasingly used by advocacy organizations: leveraging celebrity platforms not just for visibility, but for actual grassroots mobilization. Concertgoers who might not attend a rally or town hall meeting find themselves, almost incidentally, becoming informed participants in a legislative push.

## The Stakes Behind the Spotlight

For many involved in organizing and performing at these shows, the personal stories shared—whether from the stage or in quiet conversations backstage—underscore why the legislative fight matters beyond policy language. Hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity have affected communities across the country, and advocates argue that federal recognition of these crimes as distinct offenses sends an essential message about equal protection under the law.

Lauper's willingness to use her celebrity and her signature song for this cause, combined with Nelson's on-the-ground organizing work with HRC, illustrates how cultural influence and policy advocacy can intersect. The tour doesn't promise instant legislative victory, but it does something perhaps equally important: it humanizes a policy debate, ensuring that when people think about hate crimes legislation, they think not just about legal language, but about faces, names, and the fundamental plea embedded in Lauper's most famous lyric—to be seen, and accepted, in one's true colors.

*As the tour continues, both Lauper and Nelson remain committed to a vision where the concert stage becomes a launching pad for the kind of change that outlasts any single show—one where music doesn't just reflect a movement, but helps drive it forward.*
